name: Weak test: misses the None regression

steps.text: Same tiny config-service project. Look at the code first.

steps.desc: Provider: same source as the strong scenario. .get(key, "") keeps "never None" true.
Consumer: int(get_config("port")) with no None check. Downstream relies on "never None".

Weak test: only asserts get_config("port") is not None. port is always in the dict, always a str.

No get_config("nonexistent") — the missing-key branch is untested.

steps.text: Register the guarantee — GBC runs the test (born-green). port is in the dict, so it passes.

args.desc: get_config(key) always returns str, never None.

steps.text: Test passed. Register server.py → config_loader.py dependency.
Same edit as the strong scenario: drop the .get(key, "") default. Missing keys return None.

edits.oldText:
# Critical line: the "" default is what keeps "never None" true
        return self._config.get(key, "")
edits.newText:
# "Simplified": no default — missing key returns None
        return self._config.get(key)

steps.desc: After the edit: same break as the strong scenario. Present keys fine; missing keys → None.

steps.text: Can GBC catch it this time?

It cannot. The test is still green.

The weak test only covers get_config("port"). port stays in the dict and still returns "8080" with or without the default. The missing-key branch (now None) was never under test.

GBC runs your tests. Untested branches are blind spots for the gate.

Compare the strong scenario (python demo/run_demo.py run config-service-strong): one extra assert get_config("nonexistent") is not None catches this regression.
